hints: Focus on what cooling does to particle energies, most particles shift to lower energy so the peak moves left and gets taller.
Remember that $E_A$ itself does not change with temperature, so look straight up the $E_A$ line to compare old and new curves.
Think about the area to the right of $E_A$ at lower temperature, fewer particles can overcome the barrier so the new curve must sit lower there.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the axes mean**

Think of this graph as a census of energies. The x-axis is energy and the y-axis tells you how many particles have that energy.

The mark at $E_A$ is the hurdle, only particles to the right of it can react.

**Apply cooling to the shape**

When temperature decreases, average energy decreases. The whole distribution squeezes to the left, the peak gets higher and narrower, but the total area stays the same.

$$\text{lower T} \rightarrow \text{peak shifts left and up, tail to the right drops}$$

**Find the new value at the same $E_A$**

$E_A$ is fixed by the reaction, not by temperature, so we stay on the same vertical dashed line. Because the high-energy tail drops on cooling, the new curve must cross that line at a lower number of particles than the cross mark.

That is a point directly below the original cross on the $E_A$ line, where far fewer particles have enough energy to react.

options.A: Point A is to the left of $E_A$ and at a similar height. At lower temperature the curve at energies just below $E_A$ would actually be higher or shifted, but the question asks for the value exactly at $E_A$, so A is the wrong energy.
options.B: Point B is above the original cross at $E_A$. This would mean more particles have energy equal to $E_A$ after cooling, which is opposite to what happens. This is the effect of heating, not cooling.
options.C: Point C is to the right of $E_A$. It does not lie on the $E_A$ line at all, so it cannot show the number with energy equal to $E_A$. It also suggests more high-energy particles, which fits heating.
options.D: Point D lies exactly on the $E_A$ line but below the original cross. This matches cooling perfectly: $E_A$ is unchanged, but the high-energy tail is lower, so fewer particles have energy equal to or greater than $E_A$.
